name: plf::list
workload: Insertion, erasure, iteration, sort, reverse, remove/remove_if, unique, clear and destruction, averaged across 5 element types (char through large structs) using the project's own benchmark harness
claimed_speedup: 333% faster insertion, 57% faster erasure, 17% faster iteration, 77% faster sort, 70% faster reverse, 91% faster remove/remove_if, 63% faster unique, ~1,147,900% faster clear, ~6,350% faster destruction (averages across tested types); 20-24% faster overall in ordered use-case testing
tradeoffs: Node-based like std::list, so no contiguous storage or random access; the huge clear()/destruction figures are driven by trivially-destructible fast paths and not representative of typical mixed-type workloads; API is a near drop-in replacement but not fully standard-conformant in every corner case
caveats: Benchmark is the author's own harness, but it does state compiler, flags and CPU model, satisfying the tier-A bar; only libstdc++ (via MinGW) is tested, not libc++ or MSVC STL; the clear/destruction percentages are extreme outliers versus the more modest insertion/erasure numbers
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'plf::list benchmark faster than std::list github mattreecebentley' -> github.com/mattreecebentley/plf_list

name: veque
workload: Seven operation benchmarks (resize, back growth via push/pop_back, front growth via push/pop_front, arbitrary-position insertion, iteration over 2M elements, mixed random operations, copy/move reassignment), each run 3 times, per the project's performance/main.cpp harness
claimed_speedup: g++-9 -O3 totals (lower=better, microseconds): veque 2,492,954us vs std::vector 10,248,719us (~4.1x, derived from page data) and std::deque 3,480,344us (~1.4x, derived from page data); largest single-op gap is front growth: std::vector 6,685,217us vs veque 30,739us (~217x, derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: g++-9 -O3 (per benchmark source); CPU/hardware not stated
tradeoffs: Contiguous storage like vector but reserves slack at both ends, so higher memory overhead than std::vector; the ~217x front-growth figure mostly reflects std::vector's known O(n)-per-op front-insertion pathology rather than a uniform win; arbitrary-insertion and mixed-op wins are more modest (~1.4-1.9x)
caveats: First-party micro-benchmark with numbers but no stated CPU model, so it falls short of tier A even though compiler/flags are given; the standard-library vendor (presumably libstdc++ given g++-9) is not explicitly named in the source, so baseline_stdlib is left empty; the front-growth ratio is an algorithmic worst case for std::vector, not a general-purpose result
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'C++ sequence container faster than std::vector std::deque benchmark github' -> github.com/Shmoopty/veque

name: seq::tiered_vector (seq library)
workload: Insertion/deletion of single elements in the middle of the container; project's own qualitative description, no fixed element type/size stated
claimed_speedup: "Several orders of magnitude faster" than std::deque for middle insertion/deletion; project also states sorting a tiered_vector is slower than sorting a std::deque, and iterator-based random access can be slightly slower
tradeoffs: Segmented/tiered layout trades away std::deque's simplicity; the docs themselves say it is explicitly slower than std::deque for sorting and can be slower for pure random-access iteration; interface mimics std::deque but is not a literal drop-in
caveats: "Several orders of magnitude" is a qualitative claim with no exact numbers, workload size, compiler, or CPU model given; no reproducible benchmark artifact with numbers was found for this specific claim; the library's own docs conclude 'you should always benchmark with your own use cases'
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'Thermadiag seq library tiered_vector devector benchmark std::vector std::deque' -> github.com/Thermadiag/seq

name: fast_vector (sigerror/fast-vector)
workload: Google Benchmark of push_back, reserve+push_back, push_back+pop_back and emplace_back over 10,000 elements, for both trivial and non-trivial element types
claimed_speedup: Trivial types: push_back 20,126ns (std::vector) vs 9,392ns (fast_vector) ~2.1x; reserve+push_back 12,991ns vs 6,416ns ~2.0x; push_back+pop_back 12,704ns vs 9,253ns ~1.4x (all derived from page data). Non-trivial types: push_back 137,225ns vs 121,523ns ~1.1x; emplace_back 87,804ns vs 65,897ns ~1.3x (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2017 (exact optimization flags/build configuration not stated)
tradeoffs: Drops zero-initialization and exception handling (uses assertions instead) and exposes a configurable growth factor; part of the speedup comes from these relaxed semantics, so it is not a strict drop-in replacement for code relying on value-initialization or exceptions
caveats: Only tested against MSVC STL on a single Windows machine; no GCC/libstdc++ or Clang/libc++ numbers; exact compiler flags/build configuration not stated, so capped below tier A; repository has had no commits since 2019
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'martinus svector benchmark std::vector faster SVO' -> github.com/sigerror/fast-vector

name: eastl::vector (EASTL)
workload: vector<uint64> erase/insert/iteration/operator[]/push_back/sort micro-benchmarks from the original EASTL design paper's benchmark appendix
claimed_speedup: push_back ratio (std STL time / EASTL time) by platform: 1.63x on Windows/Pentium4/VC8, 2.18x on 64-bit PowerPC console/VC7, 1.02x on Linux/Pentium4/GCC4.1/libstdc++, 1.59x on Mac OS X G5 PowerPC/GCC4.0/libstdc++; operator[] on Linux/libstdc++ was 1.29x; sort on Linux/libstdc++ was 0.92x (i.e. slightly slower than std STL)
compiler_and_flags: Linux: GCC 4.1 -O3; Mac: GCC 4.0 -Os; Windows: VC8 -Og -Oi -Ot -Oy -Ob2 -GF -Gy; Console: VC7 -Ox -Ob2 -Oi -Os
hardware: Pentium 4 x86 (Windows/Linux), 64-bit PowerPC console, Mac G5 PowerPC 32-bit
stars_or_usage: 9,367 stars; used across Electronic Arts game engines
tradeoffs: Different allocator model and some container semantics diverge from the standard; results are inconsistent across operations (sort was slower on libstdc++), so 'faster' is workload- and platform-dependent rather than universal
caveats: Data is from a 2007 WG21 committee paper -- a first-party submission, not blind peer review or an independent suite; hardware (Pentium 4, G5 PowerPC) and compilers (GCC 4.0/4.1, VC7/8) are two decades old and may not reflect current toolchains/CPUs; the libstdc++ push_back win is only 2% (within noise) while the larger wins are on MSVC STL and console PowerPC STL; sort was actually slower (0.92x) on libstdc++; EASTL's current repo still ships a BenchmarkVector.cpp suite but no recent published numbers were found to confirm these ratios still hold
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'EASTL vector benchmark faster than std::vector libstdc++' -> open-std.org n2271.html, cross-referenced with github.com/electronicarts/EASTL
